title: Ask HN: How do you handle AI security for automated vulnerability management?
text: Hello World! So I am new to the world of cybersecurity, and after some back and forth with AI, I chose to use a specific tool that was recommended for automated vulnerability detection & patching, but I think the issue I encountered is something common to all similar platforms that provide AI security fixes in 2026. It proposed a fix to an issue labeled 'critical'. I gave the specific file and the fix to Gemini, and, it disagreed strongly. My trust in the platform immediately degraded. It shows in my thinking that AI security platforms for repositories are unreliable, unless you cross check every critical/high vulnerability as a human with another AI tool as well. For example, for another issue labeled 'High', the fix, I cross-checked, was correct in that case. But that that one 'critical' issue, which turned out to be not a bug at all, and certainly not critical at all, has degraded my trust strongly in AI security platforms for automated vulnerability detection & patching. Note, to prevent confusion, with automated patching I mean automated pull requests with AI-proposed fixes, pending explicit human merging. Now, I wonder what you guys use (instead, if at all), and how reliable your security tool(s) are, if at all, for automated vulnerability detection (& patching.) Happy Coding! Worldwide Wishes, Behan

title: Ask HN: How can you retrain in a field requiring expensive equipment?
text: Suppose you come up with an invention involving a highly specialized, equipment-intensive field you’re unfamiliar with, such as plasma processing or high-temperature metallurgy. You’ve already consulted experts who agree the idea is plausible, but haven’t found anyone with the relevant expertise willing to help develop a PoC. How could you acquire the necessary hands-on skills to test the invention yourself? I’ve considered switching jobs, postdocs, master’s programs, a second PhD, and shared research facilities. However, jobs and postdocs may require existing expertise, master’s programs may offer insufficient hands-on training, and independent equipment access can be prohibitively expensive (and even then, access alone may not provide the necessary training). Are there any other realistic ways to retrain in experimental fields that require specialized equipment and can’t be learned at home?

title: Ask HN: Will AI = extreme concentration of power?
text: Let's say that AI will continue to get better without being a major risk due to loss of control. I feel like in this paradigm, it will lead to: 1. Fewer and fewer people can make money via their labor. We will have a small minority of super-winners who magnify their work output 100x with AI, and most people will not be able to contribute, thus will not be able to make money. 2. More and more gains go to those who either own the best AI models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), own the infrastructure needed to serve those models (energy infrastructure, datacenters). Everyone else gets access to the benefits of AI only as much as the aforementioned groups cannot better utilize those models. So far AI models are hard to exploit as a commodity (AI companies benefit more from selling inference than using the inference themselves), but as AI models get better, an AI lab will extract more value from keeping their best models as an internal tool, and sell the outputs of those models. We are seeing the start of that with Anthropic using Claude to make discoveries in bio. 3. AI models become better at capital allocation than humans, so the job of financial planner, hedge fund manager, corporate lawyer, etc. go to swarms of agents, which only the richest will be able to afford. Every loophole, every exploit, every micro-strategy compiled into inscrutable macro-strategy will be utilized by those who can pay for millions of tokens of inference in order to turn their $30 billion into $300 billion. The tactics which humans didn't have the patience, mental energy, or tactical brilliance to employ become just another tool in an infinite toolbox the AI can exploit. It seems like all these factors spell a perfect storm to an absurdly amplified K-shaped economy, where a very very small minority of entrenched wealth dominates all economic activity, and everyone else becomes a minimally necessary human buffer, kept around for either sentimental or convenience reasons.

title: Ask HN: How to organize teams to ship AI-written code?
text: Inspired by the discussion in [1], I have an adjacent question: did your team organization and work methods change? In our company we still try to play by the (old) book: backlogs, estimates, iterations, feature teams, PR reviews, etc., but the entire thing leaks everywhere you look. There is no point in many of the old rituals, but it is also not clear how to organize ourselves now. This is different, albeit closely related, from the question of how to adjust as an IC. For example: - In our team, we almost don't see the point in PR reviews anymore, not in the old way anyway. Generated code is always good enough, and in a sense is already reviewed once by the developer who signed off (the topic is discussed in [1]). So, we are now thinking to abandon PRs, or change what we review and how we do it. We are adding more rules for code review agents and to CI. We are also thinking to replace code reviews by "concept reviews" or similar. - Speaking of those, we still try to find the right place and a process for architecture and specifications reviews. They seem to become a new subject of PR reviews in fact, but we are not there yet. - In many places we don't see the need to share the workload and knowledge between multiple developers. Reverting to the model where one developer is responsible for an entire component seems viable again. Although we are naturally worried about BusFactor=1. - Some Agile-inspired practices still work for us, namely iterative development and "deploy when ready". But the development process itself starts to resemble the old-school waterfall-ish one: think everything through, write down your constraints and your specs, design the architecture first, then (re)generate the code at will. I wonder what other practices will go away or get adopted. There are probably more examples, hopefully you get the gist. I am very interested in discussing how do we organize the teams now? title: Ask HN: Dark mode for HN please? (2026)
text: The 2020 thread does a lot: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23197966 It shows 100 solutions in light of Parkinson’s Law of Triviality. Intense opinions and discussion. It teaches about alligator energy and how they can live without food for up to two years. It teaches that this site should look like top, yet I’ve rarely seen top on a white terminal in the past two decades. This does exist, nofi. Workarounds exist, and those are “mid” janky shit shows. One I tried was an iOS app. It flashes the page between light and dark on every click. Aside from not being a solution, it’s nausea-inducing, takes 20+ steps to install, requires you to blindly trust the app without a Git repo, and requires you to change your OS. It shows that running 20 miles to solve this is what people do to get to any promise of a solution. So many of these exist that it’s just a swamp of well intended nightmares making the problem worse. HN is filled with love for fonts, styling, terminal themes, CSS madness, and quirks. Yet here I am with empty hands and little karma, with a screen that burns into my eyes at night. The last bastion of light, in more ways than intended. As with the resolution to PHP’s sleep(), going with something that keeps things running unchanged for those who don’t move, but tailoring it further for those who want it, I’d opt for two extremes for logged-in users: A: Adding a custom CSS styling text area, allowing for maximized creativity, experimentation, hacking, and freedom, and supporting any matter of taste and necessity. It is just fun, and this might be shut down due to arguments about security, bloat, resetting mistakes, and such. But it’s still the most fun and expressive option. B: Having a drop-down setting for some styles, where just inverting the whole site with two lines of CSS using `filter: invert()` works for me, or choosing whatever theme is agreed upon somewhere. We have millions of dollars’ worth of CSS talent on this site and similar amounts of LLM investment to get something tasteful, respectful, well thought out, and just great. Make it a contest. Hurt me plenty. This is not a dilemma, but I hope to inspire a move toward a native solution so I can read HN at night without the abracadabra of altering my OS, browser, trust, or, well, anything outside this site. I’m also fine with no solution to this if the answer is: You should not read HN at night for a better and healthier life. Then add that to HN policy. I didn’t find that. Sorry for bringing this up again.

title: Ask HN: Beyond traces, how do you know your agent did the job?
text: I keep going back and forth on this. Traces and logs tell me what the agent did: every tool call, retry, token, and step. That's useful when something breaks. What I'm less sure about is whether that tells me the agent actually did the right thing. A run can look clean and still miss what I wanted. Or it can "finish" without the outcome really being done. So finished and succeeded aren't the same thing. I haven't made up my mind how to check for that, but I'm experimenting a lot with extracting intents from my agent and correlating among them. Curious how you do it: - Do you capture intent and outcome explicitly (e.g. giving a tool to the agent to "declare" it), or infer them after the fact from the traces? - What kind of "questions" do you "ask" your traces?

title: Ask HN: Is Agentic Coding really faster?
text: I am trying to get a grasp of what we can do with agents. I am an avid user of agentic coding. But somehow I think I code faster by hand (by IDEs I mean). I've always had a sketch approach to coding. Where I kinda lay out the pieces of what needs to be done and then finish them in chunks. That way you keep building a mental picture of what needs doing. Lately I've noticed something - its quite fast to analyze a new code-base with agents for sure especially messy ones. But once I do get a hold of the codebase (even larger ones), I can change things by hand quite quickly. My bottleneck seems to be typing, but manipulating the mental map is a lot faster. Does this match other folks experience or am I deluding myself ?

title: Ask HN: System One models for autonomous agents
text: I've seen a few impressive demos of Typesafe's new paradigm with System One models, and it seemed really clear to me that this was probably the direction the industry, especially for autonomous agents, was headed. It's been a while though, and the major providers still seem to rely on more powerful LLMs (System Two) for all tasks, regardless of complexity. Similar to how chain of thought arose, I thought the System One/System Two Thinking Fast and Slow model was one of those human structures that fit really well onto training neural nets, and I thought that this new paradigm could really change things. That doesn't seem to be the case so far though, and I'm kind of puzzled to why this hasn't broken the industry open by now. Of course my predictions are not infallible, and one shouldn't expect much accuracy or for progress to abide by rigid schedules, but nonetheless: how come Kahneman Computer Use models aren't everywhere by now?

title: Ask HN: Why people keep posting AI-generated projects around the Internet?
text: Programming-related subreddits and other media platforms are current flooded by the waterfall of AI-generated projects. A typical post contains a problem description and the link to GitHub repo created just recently with sustainable amount of generated code in it. With the invite to review it, and to give a community feedback. The quality of the projects vary, but very often these are codebases generated in a few days solely by the AI-agentic systems with little to no human review and prior history of development and recognition. I'm asking this question not out of critiques. I genuinely don't understand motivation and the roots of this phenomena. Asking for the professional code review seems to be pointless for the publisher. Many of them didn't have prior experience in the programming language in which the code has been generated. Furthermore, the code is seemingly not interested for the publisher either. It does not look to me as a good start for community-driven (F)OSS project anyway. Another motivation that I can imaging is seeking for public recognition. But considering the amount of postings, I think it's highly unlikely in the current situation even for the genuinely high-effort works. I can also assume that some are seeking for the self promotion by faking professional skills with AI assistance. That might be true for some, but the majority don't hide the fact that the presented code has been generated. It's unlikely the main motivation too. So, I completely lost in understanding on what's going on, and what steams this never-stopping process. At a first glance the author doesn't gain anything in return, and I don't understand what they are seeking for.

title: Ask HN: What Got You into Rust?
text: Back in 2024 I was experimenting with prosthetic arms and trying to figure out how to build one with an EMG sensor. The problem I kept running into was that the EMG sensor kept crashing the Arduino IDE. It spat out data at an extremely high rate, and my RAM couldn't keep up with it, being on a potato laptop. That's when I thought, "Okay, maybe let's try Rust. What's the worst that can happen?" This is the first thing I ever built in Rust: https://github.com/CLoaKY233/serial-plotter I used a sliding window: keep deleting the oldest values and keep pushing the newer ones onto the graph. It looked a bit like a snake chasing its tail, but it's what actually worked for us later at the Smart India Hackathon 2024 Hardware finals (we didn't win). Sharing something from back when trying something new and building something new felt exciting. Maybe we'll never get to build things quite the same way again :D So I'd love to hear what got you into Rust, what your first Rust project looked like, and what you've cooked since :>

title: Ask HN: Frontier Capability on Average Computers
text: I really want to find a way to get frontier-level intelligence on local hardware. I think some really cool ways to get this have been done already like the technique of spreading an LLMs weights across a fast-enough SSD and then only serving up an expert at a time on the GPU/SoC. I have this idea to make a tool that lets people download several small open-weight models and they act like experts but are different very task specific models with a harness designed to keep track of their thoughts & work to let normal hardware be able to get close to frontier (or just useful level intelligence). Basically, I want to have a model that acts like a router or decision maker where you start your chat with initially (say a coding task for example) and it decides what model does the work next. If it needs to research it writes down in an .MD what it needs to find out, if it needs to write code, another model starts working but the other models memory & work get saved to an .MD (or folder of .MDs) and lets you get real work done but completely locally. This might already be done but its just an idea I had and I wanted to see what the smart people on the internet thought or how they would approach this. I might also just be able to ask AI.

title: Ask HN: Demonstrating Skills When Everything Is a Prompt
text: I used to (and sometimes still do) love really thinking about a problem - pen and paper, whiteboards, thinking on the tornado throne, you name it. And before AI, the projects I came up with might not have been the BEST or life-changing but they were the result of me hyper-focusing on something niche for an inordinate amount of time. These days I find myself wondering if there's anything that isn't a prompt (or a few hundred) away. And if it is, what would make my skills valuable or even visible. To be clear, I'm not a pessimist. I don't think its time to till the fields for our overlords. I'm trying to understand what advice people think is still applicable and what is a relic that needs a patch or two. TL;DR: AI projects are impressive but don't always indicate skills. title: Ask HN: Are signed URL previews feasible?
text: Lots of protocols and software allow URL previews. But they have some annoying limitations: For centralized public services the server can just retrieve the preview and serve it. But for decentralized services like Mastodon either every server has to fetch the preview on its own leading to lots of traffic and potential discrepancies between the previews served by different servers or the origin home server sends the preview but now everyone has to trust that it is authentic. The home server to which a link gets posted could place anything as its preview and thereby indirectly impersonate the URL and fake its content. For E2EE messengers things are even more annoying because you do not want the servers to see the URL at all. So either all parties have to retrieve the preview on their own meaning they have to connect to a random, potentially malicious URL or only the sender does and everyone has to trust the sender that the preview is authentic which is a great opportunity for scams.^1 The perfect solution would be a standard for web servers to sign URL previews with their CA issued certificate. So that you can always proof that a preview is authentic. RFC 9421 already standardizes this. But this will not happen. There is virtually no chance of widespread adoption. So my idea is: You retrieve a webpage and record the whole TLS session including certificates, MACs and your key material like nonce and client random from the handshake. Now you use this as the basis for the URL preview. When you include your secret material from the TLS handshake anyone should be able to verify that the content is authentic from the server serving the URL due to the CA certificate and authentication of TLS traffic. Standardize the request headers and limit the response length. Just cut off everything after the limit. Define some algorithm for computing the preview that ever recipient can verify. If you want to include linked images in the preview that increases complexity but should be doable. Repeat the whole thing with the linked image and create a bundle from all requests that authenticates the preview. The downside I see is complexity and the need for the receiver to parse the preview bundle which might be attack surface. Does anything similar already exist? Am I missing something or do you think this might be feasible to implement? [1] Many messengers solve this by providing a URL preview service on the server. The client sends the URL to the messenger service which retrieves (and signs I hope) a URL preview which the client then includes in the message. This has the advantage that none of the parties of the conversation has to directly connect to an untrusted UTL. This bypasses E2EE for URLs. You can usually opt of this by disabling previews. Consider this if you did not know about this.

title: Ask HN: What Happened in DNSSEC Yesterday?
text: I have had DNSSEC verification enabled for a couple of months in systemd-resolved. Not that I am particular paranoid or do any nuclear-sensitive stuff on my machine. Don't even own any Bitcoin. An internet search brought up https://github.com/NordSecurity/nordvpn-linux/issues/1853 which also links to another one. The timing seems to match with my observation, but I don't use NordVPN. Any clues?

title: Ask HN: Can we discourage Show HNs that "ship the first draft"
text: Agents are here to stay - so slop is too. Unfortunately it's easy to vibe a plausible thing for A Show HN, so (some, not all) Show HNs demonstrate only the creator's ability to ask agents for a thing. Shipping a first draft (instead of refining it into something only you could've done) forces others to inspect the mess and decide if there's any "there" there. It offloads the work of deciding if the work is worthwhile. Badly written README; landing page full of LLMisms; a buggy mess that only works on my box.. all signs of lack of the love and craft to which the hacker ethos aspires.. Can we raise the bar? The Show HN guidelines (https://news.ycombinator.com/showhn.html) cover most of this so maybe people just need to be gently redirected / more enforcement is needed ... What if Show HN submissions require "proof-of-work", ie. here's how this goes beyond just prompting; a behind-the-scenes, if you will. Something a person has to hand-write that proves their thing is worth checking out. Or something else? But it'd be great to lift the quality of Show HNs.

title: Ask HN: Have you ever spoken truth to power?
text: A year and a half ago I heard of Arizona’s chief law enforcement officer, Attorney General Kris Mayes, going on a “listening tour”. She was taking 3-minute statements from the public. My statement said, essentially, ‘I too am concerned. But people in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones.’ I opened with a brief history of federal protections for US citizens’ civil rights, then transitioned to how modern America's civil rights crimes are perpetrated against those who can't afford an expensive attorney to represent them. I next made the case that federal intervention to protect Arizona citizens' fundamental rights is more important than ever: “Modern Arizona’s protection racket is particularly vicious to women who make the mistake of trusting their doctor.” [0] My first example was the passenger who could have been anyone’s grandmother. The second could have been anyone’s daughter. Both women were punished for having health problems that were exacerbated by their trusted doctors’ prescriptions. My statement did NOT make the AAG’s highlight reel. Technically protection rackets are one of the businesses of organized crime. When a government perpetrates crimes against its own people, those are “state crimes”. When a government looks the other way to allow private entities to perpetrate crimes, those are “state-sanctioned crimes”. There were other women who didn’t deserve what happened to them. One night I was sent to rescue a woman who’d been dumped on the streets of downtown Phoenix after the city cops found a better suspect for the petty beer thief they were looking for. I got her again, almost 2 years later - she shared how appreciative she still was that I'd helped her [1]. Another passenger spent ~9 years in minimum security prison for sharing a single opiate pill with a friend. She said the police officers laughed as they wrote her up. She’d gotten fat on prison food, and shared that other women died from neglect. Sometimes men are also not helped by being locked up for having health problems. The sister of Mr. “who are your lifelines” [2] told me about how her brother originally got locked up after he lost his job and was not able to pay his child support. California's laws were eventually changed to allow for fathers' changing economic circumstances, but that was too late for my passenger. He’d developed adult onset Type 1 diabetes during his early incarcerations, and would be a case study of the futility of using incarceration to worsen people’s health problems. HN: Have you ever spoken a truth to someone with more power than you? How do I use my recording of my statement to call for reforms to the make-work aspects of the United States' approach to health and justice? [0] The inefficiencies of Arizona’s approach to crime and punishment was a recurring theme in my experiences driving a taxi, circa 2012-2015. I wrote about some of the injustices I witnessed: America's Make-Work Sheriff: The Anachronism of Joseph Arpaio, for example: https://www.taxiwars.org/2017/09/americas-make-work-sheriff-anachronism.html [1] Ordinary Rendition: https://www.taxiwars.org/2017/10/ordinary-rendition-public-servants.html [2] This passenger came to my part of rural Arizona, got arrested again and gave my number to his sister, whom I met when she came out to rescue his cats. title: Ask HN: Is there any defense against LLM-based reverse engineering?
text: Recent news headlines [1] about LLM-based reverse engineering make it seem that anyone with a monthly subscription is capable of translating any executable into an equivalent source code representation. If this is true, then how can one guard against having their source code essentially unveiled with the correct semantic meaning of the underlying algorithms by someone with an extremely low amount of effort? I bet that using obfuscators would still not be enough. I'm distinguishing between recreating the source code of your software vs vibe coding an inexact clone without knowing your source code (which is not exactly reverse engineering). Example: Imagine it would be possible to faithfully recreate the source code of the firmware running on a foreign military device, even with correct semantic meaning of variables, functions and of the whole algorithm. On the other hand, vibe coding a clone would require that you know the underlying algorithm (or at least that you have a high-level idea of how does it work), which you don't have for such device. Does it mean that companies like Denuvo are now out of business (assuming anything can be reverse engineered with the correct semantic meaning)? [1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50028275

text: I moved my homelab into a colocation rack (proper DC deployment with redundant power) a while ago. title: Ask HN: Do you want a router that has DD-WRT pre-installed?
text: I sometimes run across comments where someone says they want an open-source router. I wonder if this is a viable idea for someone to start as a small company. What makes me hesitant is that, first, it looks like this already exists in several wireless and non-wireless routers (like the GL.iNet Flint or OpenWrt One), and second, I assume hackers would just make their own. I have been flashing DD-WRT to my routers for many years. My current setup is an Archer C9 that connects via cable to an Archer C8, which then wirelessly bridges to an R7000. All of them run DD-WRT. If I had "fun money," I would buy a low-power SFF PC with dual NICs, run OPNsense or OpenWrt, and use the wireless routers strictly as access points. Since I don't have that much to spend, I look for older DD-WRT friendly routers, usually under $30, on Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace, and flash them myself. I see that Ubiquiti and MikroTik make quality routers with proprietary OSes for around $65 new. Protectli and Netgate offer pfSense routers starting at $259.00. The GL.iNet Flint 2 is $169.00, and the OpenWrt One is $89. According to ResellBot (because eBay now requires a login to see sold listings with prices), the sold "DD-WRT Routers" generally go for under $160. These include the WRT3200ACM, Netgear AC1750, Linksys EA9300, and Linksys R7350. When I asked an AI how I would go about judging interest, building, raising funds, and manufacturing, it seems doable but expensive (said $125,000 minimum in total made up of $30,000 for regulatory approval, engineering and protoyping $10,000+) and time-consuming just to get to a "golden prototype" for demos. So if I were a "hacker" and wanted an open-source router, depending on my funds, I would either: 1. Flash DD-WRT to an existing router (used or new). 2. Buy one with it already installed, like the OpenWrt One or a Protectli device. 3. Get an SFF PC and build my own. I remember when some comments about DropBox said it was a waste because any hacker could make that. I also know DropBox was marketed to the average person and businesses. I don't really see how a hacker friendly router could take off like that unless hackers are choosing the hardware and setting up the networks for average people. And I assume that most people setting up the networks want different qualities like brand name recognition, ease and speed of purchasing equipment (Walmart or BestBuy), and the ability to point a customer or family member to the number of solid reviews and articles saying it a good router to qualify their choices. So, do you actually want a router that you can buy with DD-WRT pre-installed?

Data: whether synthetic examples ever convinced anyone, or whether it always came down to real customer data. title: Ask HN: Internal AI Language
text: LLMs have an internal language that they translate English into before predicting the next token. Like 'king' is translated into a word of an internal language that corresponds to vector [monarch, man], which allows king-man+woman=queen. Spanish is similar for the case 'queen'=reina, -ina suffix means female, but becomes irregular for king=rey. We have tried to create regular, consistent languages (loglan, lojban, ithkuil), and there seems to be one in the first layers of LLMs, derived from all text ever written. This internal language is currently expressed as vectors, but we could devise a lexicon to map them, and if we could learn it we could communicate more directly with machines, dispensing with some layers and getting rid of language ambiguities. Makes sense? Is someone working on this? It's like Arrival but with AI instead of aliens.

title: Ask HN: Is this the beginning of the end of open source?
text: If you're following the photopea incident, I'm sure you'd concur that the writing was on the wall. It's an inevitable outcome of the rise of AI in software dev. Any project that sees a semblance of success will be cloned overnight many times over and will find itself competing with its own copies. We saw glimpses of a similar situation in the past when large cloud platforms cloned popular softwares in a not a very dissimilar manner. This led to the creation of "source available" as an alternative to open source that gained some traction of its own. But since this mostly affected a few large players, open source by and itself was large unaffected still supported by large volumes of individuals driven by passion, motivated towards their craft. The concept of open source is itself something of an anomaly not seen in any other industry or at any other time in history. Partly fueled by an individual's desire to exhibit original work, and partly supported by the fact that code needs someone of an equal to work with, it still allowed authors to reap a net benefit while giving out their IP for free. LLMs have turned that picture over completely. It's not only trivial to derive, for all purposes, an exact copy of the IP while obscuring the source, it's also possible to maintain and operate the IP with a relatively low bar of expertise. But the other inconspicuous problem brought about by LLMs is that can you even claim original work any more? When no one believes that you wrote it yourself, what motivation remains to continue publishing as open source? With no net benefit to revealing your IP, will we see a revival to closed source distribution again?
